content.title: About
content.content: Agave liquid sweetener is made from the sap of the agave plant (Agave spp.). It has a mild, slightly caramel-like flavor and a high sweetness, about 1.5–2 times that of sugar. The product is often used as a sugar alternative in drinks, desserts, and cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Agave contains fructans that can act as prebiotics, supporting a healthy gut microbiome.
Agave sweetener has a lower glycemic index than regular sugar, but still contains a significant amount of fructose.
Traditionally, agave has been used in Mexican cuisine and for tequila production.
The production of agave sweetener requires minimal processing, preserving some natural nutrients.
Agave is cultivated in arid regions where many other crops struggle to grow.

items.title: Low Glycemic Index
items.content: Helps reduce rapid spikes in blood sugar compared with regular sugar.

items.title: Prebiotic Effect
items.content: Fructans may promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Mineral Content
items.content: Provides small amounts of calcium, potassium, and magnesium, beneficial for bones and muscles.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains trace amounts of B1, B2, and B6 vitamins involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Vegan Friendly
items.content: Fully plant‑based product with no animal‑derived ingredients.

items.title: High Fructose Content
items.content: Large amounts can burden the liver and may contribute to insulin resistance.

items.title: Agave Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions.

items.title: Caloric Value
items.content: Although sweeter than sugar, it still provides calories, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Not Recommended for Liver Disease
items.content: Excess fructose can increase liver load in people with liver conditions.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Agave liquid sweetener is easy to add to tea, coffee, smoothies, sauces, baked goods, and desserts. To replace 1 tablespoon of sugar, use about 2/3 tablespoon of the sweetener. Avoid heating above 120 °C to preserve flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent crystallization.

content.title: About
content.content: Bread, chapatti and roti are types of baked flatbreads made from flour, water and sometimes yeast or leavening agents. Bread is traditionally baked in an oven, while chapatti and roti are cooked on a dry skillet (tava) without added fat. These products are a major source of carbohydrates in many diets worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bread has been made for over 14,000 years; archaeological evidence shows its production in ancient Egypt.
Chapatti is the national flatbread of India; its name derives from the word “chapa,” meaning “flat.”
Roti is popular across South Asia, especially in Pakistan and Bangladesh, and is often served with curry.
Traditional sourdough breads are fermented, which enhances nutritional value and mineral absorption.
In many cultures bread is a symbol of hospitality and is used in rituals.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread, chapatti and roti provide steady energy by slowly releasing glucose into the bloodstream.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber (especially whole‑grain)
items.content: Whole‑grain breads contain fiber that supports healthy digestion and gut microbiota.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Fermentation or leavening in dough produces B1, B2, B3 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Whole‑grain flour supplies iron, magnesium and zinc.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Fiber and protein in whole‑grain breads help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience inflammation and intestinal damage from wheat bread.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread raises blood sugar quickly, which can be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Added salt and sugar
items.content: Some breads contain added salt and sugar, which may be an issue for hypertension or weight management.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercial bakery products may include flavor enhancers and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be eaten plain, spread with butter, cheese, avocado, or used for sandwiches. Chapatti and roti are often served hot, wrapped in foil, and used to scoop up sauces, curries or dal. They can also be frozen and reheated on a skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box to keep it soft. Chapatti and roti are best kept in an airtight container at room temperature for 2‑3 days, or frozen in a zip‑lock bag for later reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee, brewed, decaffeinated (5205) is a beverage made from roasted and ground coffee beans from which almost all caffeine has been removed. The flavor retains the characteristic notes of regular coffee, but without the stimulating effect.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed by water extraction or super‑critical CO₂ methods.
Most of the caffeine is removed during processing, not during brewing.
Decaffeinated coffee retains most of the antioxidants found in regular coffee.
In the United States, over 70 % of decaf coffee consumers prefer it as a brewed drink.
Several decaffeination methods exist, each influencing aroma and taste differently.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Decaf coffee contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports liver health
items.content: Studies suggest that moderate consumption of coffee, including decaf, may promote liver health.

items.title: May reduce type 2 diabetes risk
items.content: Regular intake of decaffeinated coffee is associated with a lower risk of developing diabetes.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Coffee stimulates gastric juice production, which can improve digestion.

items.title: Reduces anxiety
items.content: The absence of caffeine makes the drink suitable for people sensitive to nervous stimulation.

items.title: Residual solvents
items.content: Some decaffeination methods use chemical solvents; choose products that have undergone strict quality control.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Like regular coffee, decaf can irritate the stomach in individuals with high acidity.

items.title: Coffee allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to coffee components.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Brew decaffeinated coffee like regular coffee: use 1–2 tsp of ground coffee per 180 ml of hot water (90–95 °C) and steep for 4–5 minutes. Add milk, plant‑based alternatives, sweeteners or spices to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ground decaffeinated coffee in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep it in the refrigerator to preserve aroma.

content.title: About
content.content: Similac Alimentum is a hypoallergenic ready‑to‑feed infant formula designed for newborns and infants with heightened sensitivity to cow’s milk proteins. The formula features partially hydrolyzed protein, prebiotics, and essential vitamins and minerals to support growth and development in children at risk of allergy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Similac Alimentum was one of the first hypoallergenic formulas approved by the FDA.
The product is ready to use straight from the container, no reconstitution required.
It contains the prebiotic FOS (fructooligosaccharides) to promote a healthy gut microbiome.
The formula is lactose‑free, making it suitable for infants with lactose intolerance.
Each container typically provides 8–12 days of feeding at standard intake levels.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Hypoallergenic proteins and prebiotics help develop the immune system in infants with increased sensitivity.

items.title: Optimal growth
items.content: The formula supplies all essential macro‑ and micronutrients, including DHA, ARA, iron, and zinc, needed for brain and body development.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Partially hydrolyzed protein is easier to digest, reducing the risk of food‑related reactions.

items.title: Gut health
items.content: Prebiotics foster beneficial bacteria, improving digestive comfort.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Suitable for infants with lactose intolerance, minimizing gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Soy protein allergy
items.content: Although hypoallergenic, the formula may contain soy lecithin, which can trigger reactions in soy‑sensitive infants.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The product contains a small amount of maltose; consult a physician for infants with metabolic concerns.

items.title: Shelf‑life after opening
items.content: Once opened, the formula should be used within 48 hours to prevent bacterial growth.

items.title: Not a breast‑milk substitute
items.content: Intended only as a supplement or replacement under medical guidance, not as a universal breast‑milk alternative.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve the formula at room temperature. If refrigerated, gently warm to feeding temperature; do not freeze. Shake the bottle lightly before each use to ensure uniformity. Follow pediatrician recommendations for portion sizes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 48 hours. Discard if the product develops an off‑odor, discoloration, or unusual taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Plantain is a large tropical fruit from the banana family that is typically eaten only after cooking. When prepared without added fat it retains a soft texture and a mildly sweet flavor, similar to a ripe banana but with a more pronounced starchy base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Plantains are often called “cooking bananas” because raw they are too firm and starchy to eat.
Across cultures plantains are fried, boiled, baked, or steamed, each method giving a distinct taste.
In many African and Caribbean countries plantain is a staple carbohydrate, comparable to potatoes elsewhere.
There are several ripeness stages: green (unripe), yellow (partially ripe) and black (fully ripe), each with different sugar levels and texture.
Plantains are rich in resistant starch, which acts as a prebiotic supporting gut health.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provides slowly digestible starch that offers sustained energy and helps maintain stable blood glucose.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber and resistant starch promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Cooking without added fat keeps the dish low in calories from fat.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to banana family plants.

items.title: High glycemic index when fully ripe
items.content: Over‑ripe plantains can raise blood sugar quickly, which is important for people with diabetes.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Some varieties contain oxalates that may contribute to kidney stone formation if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Plantains can be boiled, baked, steamed, or mashed. They are commonly used in side dishes, soups, casseroles, and frittatas. Preparing them without oil preserves their natural flavor and keeps the meal lower in calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh plantains in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer, where they stay good for up to 5 days. Cooked pieces can be frozen in airtight containers for up to 3 months.

ravioli-cheese-and-spinach-filled-with-t.title: Ravioli, cheese and spinach filled, with tomato sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Ravioli are small pasta parcels filled with a mixture of cheese and spinach, served in a flavorful tomato sauce. The dough is made from wheat flour and eggs, while the filling typically includes ricotta, Parmesan, and fresh spinach, seasoned with salt, pepper, and a hint of nutmeg.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ravioli originated in Italy and have been made for over a thousand years.
The cheese‑spinach combination makes the dish a good source of calcium and iron.
The classic tomato sauce is often prepared from ripe tomatoes, garlic, and basil.
Ravioli can be frozen raw and cooked later without loss of texture or flavor.
In some Italian regions, ravioli are served with a drizzle of butter instead of tomato sauce.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Cheese and spinach provide a complete blend of animal and plant protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: High in calcium
items.content: Calcium from the cheese supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Spinach supplies non‑heme iron, which is better absorbed when paired with vitamin C from the tomato sauce.

items.title: Antioxidant rich
items.content: Tomatoes and spinach contain lycopene and lutein, antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from spinach and tomato sauce promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cheese filling may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should choose a low‑salt version.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The wheat‑based dough contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach is high in oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the ravioli hot, topped with tomato sauce. Sprinkle with grated Parmesan, add fresh basil, or drizzle a little olive oil. Suitable side dishes include a light salad or steamed vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh ravioli can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Frozen ravioli retain quality for up to 3 months; cook directly from frozen in boiling water without thawing.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey wing is a piece of poultry meat that contains both protein and a modest amount of fat. When boiled, the skin becomes soft and edible, while the meat stays tender and mildly flavored. Wings are commonly used in soups, stews, or served as a standalone dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey wings are rich in collagen, which supports skin and joint health.
In the United States, turkey consumption spikes around holidays, especially Thanksgiving.
The skin of turkey contains more fat than the meat, but boiling releases some of it into the broth, enhancing flavor.
Turkey wings are popular in Asian cuisines for making stocks and sauces.
There are many preparation methods: from simple boiling to roasting with spices.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Turkey wing provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Essential minerals
items.content: Wings supply iron, zinc, and phosphorus, needed for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Ideal for low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugars.

items.title: Collagen and gelatin
items.content: The skin releases gelatin during cooking, which can benefit joints and digestion.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the wings are seasoned with salt, they can become a source of excess sodium.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; proper cooking temperatures are essential.

items.title: Fat in the skin
items.content: Consuming large amounts of skin can increase the calorie density of the dish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey wings can be enjoyed hot or cold. They are often served as an appetizer, sliced into bite‑size pieces. The skin is edible after boiling and adds a pleasant texture. Pair them with yogurt‑based dips, mustard, or soy‑based sauces for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked wings in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a sealed bag for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Soybean vermicelli (2216) is a thin noodle made from whole soybeans that are milled into flour and formed into long strands. The product has a neutral taste, light texture, and a high content of plant protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soybeans are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for over 5,000 years.
Soybean vermicelli is often used in Asian cuisine as an alternative to wheat noodles.
The product is completely gluten‑free, making it suitable for people with celiac disease.
Soy is rich in isoflavones, which may have beneficial effects on hormonal balance.
Vermicelli cooks quickly—usually 3–5 minutes of boiling.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: A serving provides about 20 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other noodles, soybean vermicelli contains very little saturated fat.

items.title: Source of isoflavones
items.content: Isoflavones have antioxidant properties and may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for individuals with gluten intolerance or celiac disease.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to soy proteins.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Soy contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in excess.

items.title: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs)
items.content: Most soybeans worldwide are GMO; choose non‑GMO labeled products if preferred.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the vermicelli in salted water for 3–5 minutes, then add to soups, salads, stir‑fries, or use as a base for cold dishes. It pairs well with vegetables, tofu, seafood, and soy‑based sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry vermicelli in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent moisture and mold.
